claims.text: A predictive approach incorporating atomic-scale disorder and mass-fluctuation descriptors will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than averaged-property methods.
HfNbTaTiZr is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
CrMnFeCoNi is an equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
The target materials are considered in an as-synthesized state before microstructural modification.
The proposed model uses local lattice distortions, disorder parameters, and mass fluctuations as phonon-transport descriptors.
Standardized synthesis by methods such as sintering or quenching will provide reproducible microstructures.
Chemical and microstructural heterogeneity, including multiphase structures and local lattice distortions, enhances phonon scattering.
Configurational disorder influences local vibrational modes.
Mass fluctuations increase or otherwise modify phonon-scattering rates in HEAs.
Representing disorder-related phonon scattering enables more precise estimation of phonon-scattering rates.
Traditional predictive methods rely on average bulk properties and do not explicitly represent atomic-scale disorder and mass fluctuations.
The proposed approach will forecast lower thermal-conductivity values than traditional averaged-property methods.
The proposed approach will reduce phonon-thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to conventional models.
Alloys identified by the approach will exhibit measurably lower thermal conductivity experimentally.
The approach is primarily applicable to compositionally complex alloys with substantial atomic-size differences, mass differences, and disorder.
The approach may not apply to simpler, less chemically complex alloys.
The cited studies provide evidence that processing, environment, and temperature can affect phases or microstructural state in the named HEAs.
The exact quantitative improvement in prediction accuracy cannot be established without extensive comparison to experimental thermal-conductivity data.
TDTR can be used in the proposed benchmark to measure phonon thermal conductivity at application-relevant temperatures.

A failure to achieve a statistically significant 20% reduction in prediction error, or a failure of measured conductivity to correlate with predicted microstructural features, would falsify the hypothesis.
